text: Explain four characteristics of a successful entrepreneur.
context: Santhosh is a skilled carpenter starting RF as a sole trader, a completely new business.
caseStudy:
Recycled Furniture (RF)

Santhosh is a skilled carpenter. He wants to be an entrepreneur and start up a small business called RF. Santhosh will repair and recycle furniture which people no longer want, such as tables and chairs. Santhosh will operate RF as a sole trader.

Santhosh has produced a business plan which includes the business objectives and a forecast break-even chart for RF's first month of trading. Santhosh has calculated he will need $5000 start-up capital for new tools, to rent a workshop and for promotional activities. Santhosh wants to sell the recycled furniture to RF's target market of low-income families. It will be important to keep costs low so the furniture can be sold at a low price.

Santhosh has already employed a Marketing Manager. He will also need to recruit 9 other employees: 3 skilled carpenters and 6 unskilled school leavers. Santhosh and the skilled carpenters will train the unskilled school leavers to repair and recycle the furniture. At the start of each day Santhosh will communicate with his employees to ensure they know their daily work tasks. Santhosh knows that having a well-motivated workforce will be important to RF.

Appendix 1 — Email from Santhosh to Marketing Manager, 31 March 2024:
I know we will need to spend some of my start-up capital on promotional activities to raise awareness and encourage purchases. I am considering: (1) a 10% discount on a customer's first purchase, or (2) free delivery on all products purchased, transported directly to customers' homes.

Appendix 2 — Forecast break-even chart for RF's first month:
Break-even output = 10 items; Fixed costs = $50/month; Total revenue at break-even = $180; Total cost at break-even = $130; forecast sales = 20 items/month.

ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per characteristic (max 4) + 1 additional mark per explanation.

Characteristics: self-confident — to convince investors to provide finance; creative — to develop ideas different from existing products/services; hard-working — long hours needed for success; risk-taker — prepared to lose invested capital; also valid: innovative, effective communicator, independent, determined/perseverance.

text: Explain four reasons why governments support the start-up of new businesses.

caseStudy:
Authentic Foods (AF)

Sam started up his own business, AF, 6 years ago in country X. He received government support. Sam used to live in country A. When he moved to country X he could not find meals from his original country. Sam decided to use recipes from country A to make meals in his kitchen and sell them to people in the local area.

As demand increased Sam set up 5 street market stalls across Main City. Many customers buy his meals because they are traditional and of high quality. There are no other businesses in country X that produce these meals.

Two years ago Sam formed a business partnership with his brother. They used retained profit from the business to invest in a factory to produce meals on a larger scale. AF now has 10 skilled production employees to make the meals in the factory.

AF imports 90% of the ingredients for its meals from country A. AF could buy some ingredients locally at a cheaper price but this may change the taste of the meals. Food production businesses in country X usually buy their ingredients locally. However, most manufactured consumer products in country X are imported, so changes in the exchange rate affect their prices.

AF's factory has operated profitably since it opened. There is high demand for AF's meals, especially in Main City where many workers used to live in country A. Sam wants to expand the factory and must decide whether to increase output by investing in new technology ($50,000) or buying more of their existing equipment ($25,000). Sam is also considering introducing a new meal to the AF range.

Appendix 1 — Three legal controls being introduced in country X: increase in minimum wage (AF already pays above minimum); additional health and safety regulations (requiring training/equipment); employees limited to a maximum of 50 hours/week (production employees currently work 40, sometimes up to 60, hours/week when busy).

Appendix 2 — Email from Sam to his brother, 6 January 2024:
There are 100,000 people from country A currently employed in country X; 60% earn a high income. Our traditional meals make customers feel at home, which should keep this segment loyal. Proposed marketing mix for the new meal: penetration pricing; sold through food retailers in Main City; advertised via social media.

Appendix 3 — Cost and revenue data for two new meals:
Meal 1: ingredient cost $4/meal; additional fixed costs $6000/month; price $10/meal; forecast sales 2000/month.
Meal 2: ingredient cost $3/meal; additional fixed costs $2000/month; price $5/meal; forecast sales 5000/month.
ms:

Reasons: reduces unemployment via new jobs; increases competition, encouraging efficiency; provides social benefits (some start-ups become social enterprises); provides specialist/niche goods larger businesses don't offer; increases output/GDP; increases variety of goods/services; increases tax revenue; small businesses may grow into large ones.

caseStudy:
Authentic Foods (AF)

Sam started up his own business, AF, 6 years ago in country X. He received government support. Sam used to live in country A. When he moved to country X he could not find meals from his original country. Sam decided to use recipes from country A to make meals in his kitchen and sell them to people in the local area.

As demand increased Sam set up 5 street market stalls across Main City. Many customers buy his meals because they are traditional and of high quality. There are no other businesses in country X that produce these meals.

Two years ago Sam formed a business partnership with his brother. They used retained profit from the business to invest in a factory to produce meals on a larger scale. AF now has 10 skilled production employees to make the meals in the factory.

AF imports 90% of the ingredients for its meals from country A. AF could buy some ingredients locally at a cheaper price but this may change the taste of the meals. Food production businesses in country X usually buy their ingredients locally. However, most manufactured consumer products in country X are imported, so changes in the exchange rate affect their prices.

AF's factory has operated profitably since it opened. There is high demand for AF's meals, especially in Main City where many workers used to live in country A. Sam wants to expand the factory and must decide whether to increase output by investing in new technology ($50,000) or buying more of their existing equipment ($25,000). Sam is also considering introducing a new meal to the AF range.

Appendix 1 — Three legal controls being introduced in country X: increase in minimum wage (AF already pays above minimum); additional health and safety regulations (requiring training/equipment); employees limited to a maximum of 50 hours/week (production employees currently work 40, sometimes up to 60, hours/week when busy).

Appendix 2 — Email from Sam to his brother, 6 January 2024:
There are 100,000 people from country A currently employed in country X; 60% earn a high income. Our traditional meals make customers feel at home, which should keep this segment loyal. Proposed marketing mix for the new meal: penetration pricing; sold through food retailers in Main City; advertised via social media.

Appendix 3 — Cost and revenue data for two new meals:
Meal 1: ingredient cost $4/meal; additional fixed costs $6000/month; price $10/meal; forecast sales 2000/month.
Meal 2: ingredient cost $3/meal; additional fixed costs $2000/month; price $5/meal; forecast sales 5000/month.
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per way (max 2) + max 3 additional marks per explanation, one applied to context.

Ways: decreases the cost of imports, allowing lower prices and more competitive/higher sales; may free up more consumer income for AF's meals as other imported goods get cheaper too; AF may gain a competitive edge over local competitors who don't import (unaffected by the appreciation); profit margins may rise due to lower raw material costs.

Application: meals; workers from another country; food recipes; 90% ingredients imported; partnership; 100,000 workers; produced in own kitchen originally; new technology under consideration; high demand; no similar local competitors.

text: Explain four reasons why a business might remain small.
context: CC is a sole trader cookie business started 5 years ago by Sam, kept deliberately small, with 10 production employees and 5 shop employees, selling high-quality cookies from one shop in the city centre.
caseStudy:
Chosen Cookies (CC)

Sam started CC 5 years ago in country P. He set up as a sole trader because he wanted to keep the business small. CC makes different types of cookies and sells them in its own shop in the city centre. Sam's cookies are high-quality and often purchased by customers for special occasions such as birthdays or weddings. Sam is reviewing the pricing method he uses as he wants to sell more cookies. Sam also knows packaging used for the cookies is important.

CC's cookies are produced by batch production using specialised baking equipment. The ingredients are purchased regularly so they are fresh. CC has 10 employees producing the cookies and 5 employees in its shop. Sam wants to recruit an Operations Manager to oversee the production of the cookies to give him more time to be with his family.

Sam is developing new cookies. He has two options to choose between. These are outlined in Appendix 3. He plans to start selling these new cookies to other retail shops in country P. These retail shops already sell a variety of cookies from different manufacturers.

There are many reasons why a business might need finance. Sam is reviewing CC's finances and is considering taking out a bank loan.

Appendix 1 — Advert for CC's cookies:
"Treat your family and friends to high-quality CC cookies to celebrate a special occasion. Personalised messages can be added to your cookie. The cookies can be purchased in CC's shop in the city centre."

Appendix 2 — Newspaper article in Main News, 1 October 2024:
The government has announced that interest rates will decrease from 1st November 2024. The decrease will affect many businesses and consumers in country P. Taxes will also change and will increase from 1st April 2025. The government plans to use some of the additional tax revenue to increase payments to people on the lowest incomes.

Appendix 3 — Forecast information for CC's two options for the new cookies:
Option 1: Forecast sales 8000 cookies/month; Variable costs $0.50/cookie; Additional fixed costs $3000/month; Possible price $1/cookie; Forecast sales growth High.
Option 2: Forecast sales 1500 cookies/month; Variable costs $2/cookie; Additional fixed costs $3000/month; Possible price $5/cookie; Forecast sales growth Low.
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per reason (max 4) + 1 additional mark per explanation.

Reasons (any four): product/service specialised or personal/customised — not suitable for large-scale production; small market size / niche market / low demand; owner's choice — work-life balance, less stress, satisfied with performance; easier to manage/control — owner makes decisions, may lack skills to manage larger business; owner knows all employees — personal relationships, easier communication; lack of finance / fewer finance options; maintains close customer relations — loyalty, face-to-face service; not willing to take more risk/responsibility; market dominated by large competitors restricting growth.

Example: "The product is specialised (1) and therefore not suitable to be produced on a large scale (1)."

context: CC sells high-quality, personalised cookies for special occasions from its own shop; considering how to price its existing product range.
caseStudy:
Chosen Cookies (CC)

Sam started CC 5 years ago in country P. He set up as a sole trader because he wanted to keep the business small. CC makes different types of cookies and sells them in its own shop in the city centre. Sam's cookies are high-quality and often purchased by customers for special occasions such as birthdays or weddings. Sam is reviewing the pricing method he uses as he wants to sell more cookies. Sam also knows packaging used for the cookies is important.

CC's cookies are produced by batch production using specialised baking equipment. The ingredients are purchased regularly so they are fresh. CC has 10 employees producing the cookies and 5 employees in its shop. Sam wants to recruit an Operations Manager to oversee the production of the cookies to give him more time to be with his family.

Sam is developing new cookies. He has two options to choose between. These are outlined in Appendix 3. He plans to start selling these new cookies to other retail shops in country P. These retail shops already sell a variety of cookies from different manufacturers.

There are many reasons why a business might need finance. Sam is reviewing CC's finances and is considering taking out a bank loan.

Appendix 1 — Advert for CC's cookies:
"Treat your family and friends to high-quality CC cookies to celebrate a special occasion. Personalised messages can be added to your cookie. The cookies can be purchased in CC's shop in the city centre."

Appendix 2 — Newspaper article in Main News, 1 October 2024:
The government has announced that interest rates will decrease from 1st November 2024. The decrease will affect many businesses and consumers in country P. Taxes will also change and will increase from 1st April 2025. The government plans to use some of the additional tax revenue to increase payments to people on the lowest incomes.

Appendix 3 — Forecast information for CC's two options for the new cookies:
Option 1: Forecast sales 8000 cookies/month; Variable costs $0.50/cookie; Additional fixed costs $3000/month; Possible price $1/cookie; Forecast sales growth High.
Option 2: Forecast sales 1500 cookies/month; Variable costs $2/cookie; Additional fixed costs $3000/month; Possible price $5/cookie; Forecast sales growth Low.
ms:
12 marks. Levels-based marking.

Cost-plus: Advantages — easy to apply (add mark-up to costs); different mark-ups possible in different markets; ensures profit on each cookie. Disadvantages — only profitable if sufficient sales; time-consuming to research ingredient costs; no incentive to reduce costs; price may be too high to stay competitive.
Promotional: Advantages — low price attracts customers for occasions like birthdays; helps launch into new markets/shops; clears unwanted perishable inventory; renews interest if sales falling. Disadvantages — low profit per cookie; customers may resist later price rises; may signal low quality; risk of price competition.
Competitive: Advantages — high sales likely at competitor-matched prices; avoids price competition, steady revenue; can compete on quality instead. Disadvantages — cookies may seem indistinguishable from competitors; high research costs to track competitor prices; high-quality cookies may need higher prices than competitors, hurting sales.

Valid recommendations: cost-plus ensures guaranteed profit per cookie; OR promotional builds attention and renews interest; OR competitive keeps CC's higher-quality cookies chosen at a similar price to competitors.

text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages of BB being a public limited company.
context: BB is a public limited company manufacturing bicycles, planning to raise finance for a new factory and expansion into becoming a multinational.
caseStudy:
Big Bikes (BB)

BB is a public limited company which manufactures bicycles in country X. It produces a range of bicycles for different age groups from young children to adults. BB's main market is in country X where it sells its bicycles through specialist bicycle shops. It also exports 30% of its output.

BB uses flow production and employs 100 production workers in its factory. These production workers are paid $10 per hour. BB has high labour turnover as its employees are not well-motivated. BB has a flat organisational structure with a short chain of command (Managing Director → Operations/Finance/HR/Marketing/R&D Directors → assistants/100 production employees; total 150 employees).

BB's sales have increased every year since it was set up 25 years ago. However, sales of bicycles in country X have been growing more slowly in the last year. BB's best-selling children's bicycle is now in the maturity stage of the product life cycle and sales of this product have not grown for the last 3 years. BB's Marketing Director wants to use an extension strategy to boost sales for this product rather than stopping production.

BB wants to start selling its products in new markets in other countries. It is also going to become a multinational company as it plans to manufacture, as well as sell, its bicycles in other countries. This decision will affect BB's different stakeholder groups. BB needs to choose between country A and country B when deciding where to locate its first new factory.

Appendix 2 — Information about the two countries for BB's first new factory:
Country A: 70% of raw materials available locally, cost $350/bicycle; low unemployment, wage cost $300/bicycle; many competitors, selling price $1000/bicycle.
Country B: 40% of raw materials available locally, cost $175/bicycle; high unemployment, wage cost $100/bicycle; few competitors, selling price $400/bicycle.

Appendix 3 — Extracts from financial statements of BB and its main competitor:
BB: ROCE 30%; long-term bank loan $10m; acid test ratio 1.3; revenue $120m; gross profit $60m; profit $6m.
Main competitor: ROCE 15%; long-term bank loan $60m; acid test ratio 0.67; revenue $200m; gross profit $120m; profit $40m.
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per advantage/disadvantage (max 4) + 1 additional mark per explanation applied to context.

Advantages: can sell shares to public — raises capital for new factory; rapid expansion possible via large capital raises — becoming multinational; limited liability encourages investment; continuity.
Disadvantages: accounts public — competing bike manufacturers can see them; pressure to pay large dividends — restricts planned expansion; risk of takeover/loss of control; more complex accounting/reporting requirements.

Application: new factory; bikes; flow production; wants to become multinational; exports 30%; target market adults and children; 100 production workers; sells through specialist bike shops; high labour turnover; sales increased every year since set up.

text: Explain two ways the slump in country P's economy may be affecting SA.
context: Country P's economy is in a slump (Appendix 1), forecast to move into growth phase in 2025. SA manufactures sustainable cotton clothing and has been trading 30 years.
caseStudy:
Sustainable Attire (SA)

SA is a public limited company which has been trading for 30 years in country P. It manufactures clothes which are made from sustainable cotton. SA has a brand image for protecting the environment and for producing high-quality products. SA's objectives are to increase profit, to increase market share and to survive.

SA has one factory in country P and uses batch production to manufacture its clothes. It employs 500 production workers. All of SA's raw materials, including cotton, come from sustainable sources. These raw materials are purchased regularly as SA uses just-in-time (JIT) inventory control. The Operations Director is considering whether quality control or quality assurance is the best method to use to achieve quality production.

SA's clothes are sold in country P through its own shops. Its products can also be purchased online from SA's website and delivered directly to customers. The Operations Director knows that the role of packaging is important.

Appendix 1 — Newspaper article in Main News, 1 October 2024 ("Slump nearly over"):
Many businesses in country P have been affected by the economy being in a slump. Government forecasts suggest that the economy will move out of the slump and into the growth phase of the business cycle in 2025. This will be good news for businesses that have found it difficult to survive.

Appendix 2 — Email from the Managing Director to the Human Resources Director, 2 October 2024:
Labour turnover in our factory is low. We have a reputation for being a good employer and our production workers are well motivated. I am pleased that we have not made any of our production workers redundant during the slump. We have been able to keep them all by reducing the hours they work. Our production workers have been willing to change from full-time contracts to part-time contracts. This has helped us to keep our experienced skilled workers.

Appendix 3 — Extract from SA's income statements for 2023 and 2024 (forecast):
2023: Revenue $20m; Cost of sales $5m; Expenses $10m; Profit $5m.
2024 (forecast): Revenue $30m; Cost of sales $10m; Expenses $14m; Profit $6m.
ms:

text: Explain two reasons why customers might buy from ES rather than from one of its competitors.
context: ES is a sole trader boat manufacturer in country X with 12 skilled employees. It has a well-known brand and a reputation for high quality. ES has been voted 3rd best boat builder in country X. It promotes in sailing magazines and is considering social media. ES has a flat organisational structure with a short chain of command.
caseStudy:
Exceptional Sailing (ES) — Case Study Summary

Tim worked at a large boat manufacturer in country X for 20 years. He is highly skilled in building boats. Tim decided to start his own business, called ES, 4 years ago. He currently operates as a sole trader.

ES only makes and sells boats in country X. It has become established as a well-known brand with a reputation for high quality. ES has 12 skilled employees including an assistant who helps Tim to run the business. ES has a flat organisational structure with a short chain of command.

ES has grown quickly and Tim plans to expand the business further by selling his boats to customers in other countries. He is aware that there are opportunities and threats of globalisation, especially as tariffs and quotas on boats and their component parts have been removed both in country X and in other countries.

Tim plans to take out a bank loan to help fund the expansion. His two brothers will also invest in the business. One brother has experience of financial management, the other is skilled in IT. Tim will need to decide whether ES should become a partnership or a private limited company.

Tim wants to manufacture a new boat and needs to choose between Product A and Product B. ES currently promotes its boats in sailing magazines. Tim is considering using social media to promote his new boat to a wider market. Tim will need to recruit 4 new employees who will require training — either on-the-job at ES or off-the-job at college two days a week.

Appendix 1 — Advertisement for ES:
"Choose ES to build your boat. Excellent quality workmanship and boats built to your design. We have been voted the third best boat builder in country X. You could use a larger company to build your boat, but we offer so much more! Contact us for further information."

Appendix 2 — Two new products ES could produce:
Product A (large boat): Price $500,000; Additional fixed costs $400,000/year; Variable costs $450,000/boat; Forecast sales year 1: 9 boats; Sales forecast: growth in other countries.
Product B (small boat): Price $200,000; Additional fixed costs $400,000/year; Variable costs $180,000/boat; Forecast sales year 1: 24 boats; Sales forecast: growth in country X.

Key calculations:
Product A: Contribution = $50,000/boat; Break-even = 8 boats; Margin of safety = 1 boat; Profit (9 boats) = $50,000.
Product B: Contribution = $20,000/boat; Break-even = 20 boats; Margin of safety = 4 boats; Profit (24 boats) = $80,000.

Appendix 3 — Financial information for 2024 (from Tim's email to brothers):
- Revenue increased by 50%
- Gross profit margin: 65%
- Profit: $100,000
- Current ratio: 2
- Acid test ratio: 0.5
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per reason (max 2) + max 3 additional marks per explanation — at least one must be applied to context.

Reasons (any two):
- ES has a well-known brand name — easy for customers to identify — stands out from competitors — more likely to choose ES over less well-known ones
- Customers assured of the quality they expect — attracts more customers — boat less likely to have faults
- Customers may think quality higher than unbranded products — more willing to pay higher price — confident boats manufactured by skilled employees
- ES has a good reputation — customers confident ES is reliable — reassured ES will meet their needs
- ES products may be cheaper than competitors

Application: boats; 20 years experience; sole trader; sailing; 12 skilled employees; 4 new employees; high quality; well-known brand; voted 3rd best; promotion in sailing magazines; information from Appendix 2 or 3.

Example: 'ES has a brand name that is well-known so makes it easy for customers to identify it (1) as its brand name makes the business stand out from competitors (1) so customers more likely to choose ES over less well-known competitors (1) when buying a new boat (app).'

Partnership — Advantages: easy to set up — few legal requirements — reducing costs; more capital invested — three partners investing own money; share responsibilities — one brother has financial management experience; more new ideas from three partners; complete privacy — no need to share financial details; all owners motivated as their business.
Partnership — Disadvantages: unlimited liability — personal possessions at risk; no continuity — business ends if partner leaves; partners may disagree — slower decisions; one partner's actions bind all others.

Private limited company — Advantages: separate legal identity — company can be sued not owners; can sell shares to family/friends — larger capital for boat expansion; limited liability — will not lose personal possessions; cannot be taken over without shareholder consent.
Private limited company — Disadvantages: accounts not private — competitors may access; not easy to transfer shares; legal formalities to operate — accounts audited and registered — increases costs for ES; legal formalities setting up — takes time and money.

Valid recommendations:
- Partnership: brothers have complete control, keep all profit, full privacy. Should not become Ltd as competitors could access accounts and audit costs increase.
- Private limited company: three brothers have protection of limited liability — if ES goes bankrupt will not lose personal possessions, only money invested.

Cap at Level 2 without justified recommendation.

text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages to Jemi of buying a franchise.
caseStudy:
Vegan Veg (VV) — Case Study Summary

Jemi is planning to buy a franchise called VV, a restaurant brand that only serves vegan meals. The meals do not contain any ingredients made from animal products. Market segmentation is important to VV. There has been an increasing trend for people to eat vegan meals.

Jemi will need to decide the best location for her restaurant. There are three possible locations outlined in Appendix 2. The restaurant will serve a wide range of vegan meals and Jemi will purchase ingredients, including fruit and vegetables, directly from local suppliers.

Jemi will employ a chef to cook the meals. The chef will be expected to work 40 hours a week. Jemi has identified the two best applicants (Tianna and Vea). As well as a chef, Jemi plans to employ another 3 people to help in the kitchen and 8 people to serve customers. Jemi is considering using job enrichment or giving a discount on meals to keep employees motivated.

Jemi is going to use her own capital of $50000 to buy the franchise, but will also need external finance. Jemi knows that the profitability and liquidity ratios for her restaurant will be important for success.

Appendix 1 — Two applicants for the position of chef:
Tianna: Wage $12/hr. Fully qualified chef, 20 years experience in several restaurants. Training: at another VV restaurant, cost $1000, 2 weeks.
Vea: Wage $8/hr. Part-qualified chef, 10 years as assistant chef in vegan restaurants. Training: chef training course at college, cost $10000, 10 weeks.

Appendix 2 — Three possible locations:
Location A: On a main road in the centre of Main City. Popular with tourists and workers. Many restaurants. Low unemployment.
Location B: In a shopping mall on the edge of Main City. Visited mainly by families. Mall open 06:00-18:00. No restaurants in the mall. Low unemployment.
Location C: In a small town. High unemployment. Several restaurants visited by many local people.

Appendix 3 — Newspaper article (3 May 2025):
A recent government report said everyone should eat more fruit and vegetables — particularly important for children and for a long life. Eating less meat is also good for the environment. Five years ago only 10% of the population ate vegan meals; this has increased to 25% and the trend is forecast to continue. Many well-known restaurants are adding vegan meals to their menus and new vegan restaurants are opening. However, it is getting more difficult to find reliable suppliers of fruit and vegetables, and restaurants now have to buy from suppliers further away.
ms:
Award 1 mark for each advantage/disadvantage (max 2 advantages / max 2 disadvantages). Award max 1 additional mark for each explanation applied to context.

Advantages:
- Risk of business failure is much reduced — brand is well-known with people who like eating vegan meals
- Franchisor pays for national advertising — reducing promotion costs for the restaurant
- Supplies obtained from central sources / quality assured by franchisor — less need to research plant-based ingredient suppliers
- Fewer decisions to be made
- Training for employees and management provided/arranged by franchisor
- Banks more willing to lend as risk of failure is lower

Disadvantages:
- Less independence / franchisor imposes strict controls — which meals to sell
- Unable to make decisions to suit local areas — some local vegetables may be more popular than others nationally
- Licence fee must be paid to franchisor — costs $50000
- Local advertising still has to be paid for by franchisee
- Royalty payment made to franchisor each year

Application: restaurant; vegan target market; plant-based ingredients; meals; fruit and vegetables; $50000; chefs; working 40 hours a week; 12 employees; increasing trend for people eating vegan meals.

text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages of a business being a private limited company.
context: LB is a large private limited company started 20 years ago in country X. It manufactures luxury bathroom products sold to specialist retail shops.
caseStudy:
Luxury Bathrooms (LB) — Case Study Summary

LB is a large private limited company started 20 years ago in country X. It manufactures luxury bathroom products (baths, showers, basins) sold to specialist retail shops. LB has recently introduced new machinery. It has grown each year benefiting from financial, purchasing, and managerial economies of scale. The luxury bathroom market in country X is very competitive.

LB plans to produce a new range of bathroom products and is using primary market research to decide which to manufacture. It must also choose a distribution channel: specialist retail shops (existing) or directly via its website. LB currently only uses its website for information, not sales.

LB wants to enter the luxury bathroom market in country Y, planning to build a factory there in 2026, likely financed by a bank loan. It needs to communicate expansion plans to all employees.

Appendix 2 — Redundancy email data:
Redundancy payment = 1 week's wages per year employed at LB.
- Naga: Supervisor 15 years, employed 20 years, $400/week. Understands all production tasks.
- Reeta: Supervisor 2 years, employed 2 years, $350/week. 10 yrs competitor experience, already knows new machinery.
- Amy: Supervisor 5 years, employed 14 years, $375/week. Loyal, worked hard for promotion, can repair machinery.

Appendix 3 — Country Y context (City News, Sept 2025):
Economy in country Y is growing, consumer incomes rising, increasing demand for luxury home products forecast to continue. Many local businesses manufacture bathroom products. Government aware multinational companies considering locating in country Y — both benefits and drawbacks exist.
ms:
8 marks total. Award 1 mark per advantage/disadvantage (max 2 advantages, max 2 disadvantages) + 1 additional mark per explanation. No application marks for this question.

Advantages (award any two):
- Separate legal identity: company can be sued but not usually the owners personally
- Can sell shares to family/friends to raise capital — larger amounts than sole trader/partnership possible
- Limited liability: owners will not lose personal possessions if business cannot pay debts
- Cannot be taken over without shareholder consent
- Continuity on death of owner

Disadvantages (award any two):
- Accounts not private: competitors may access them
- Cannot sell shares to public/stock exchange — not easy to transfer shares so family/friends may be less willing to buy
- Legal formalities to operate: accounts must be audited and registered with government — takes time and increases costs
- Legal formalities setting up: must complete paperwork to register — takes time and money

Example full answer (2 marks): 'Cannot sell shares to the public on the stock exchange (1) as it is not easy to transfer/sell shares so family and friends may be less willing to buy shares in the first place (1).'

text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages to Philip of changing PF from a sole trader business to a private limited company.
caseStudy:
Philip Flop (PF) — Case Study Summary

Philip started PF 10 years ago as a sole trader in country X. PF makes shoes out of natural rubber. Philip used $100 000 of his own money to start up PF. The business has been very successful. Last year Philip changed PF from a sole trader business to a private limited company because he wanted to grow the business.

PF employs 20 workers to make the shoes. They are paid a weekly wage based on the number of hours worked. Philip often has to recruit new production workers as the jobs are boring. Other local businesses pay a higher wage for similar work. Philip needs to improve the motivation of PF's employees and has to decide the best way to do this.

Philip wants to build a new factory to produce a new range of shoes. PF's products will still be made from natural rubber which is grown in the local area. The bank has agreed to provide a loan to finance the building of the new factory.

Philip needs to choose a suitable location for the new factory and is considering: availability of raw materials, transport links, and government influence.

PF operates in a very competitive market. Philip will need to make a decision about how to promote the new range of shoes in a mass market.

Philip's sister is a successful entrepreneur and is considering investing in PF. She is using the extracts from PF's statements of financial position to help her decide.

Appendix 1 — Advertisement for PF's shoes:
"Natural rubber from local forests is used in the production of all our shoes. We use sustainable sources of raw materials unlike our competitors which use imported artificial rubber. Buy your first pair today and you will never buy a different brand again!"

Appendix 2 — Newspaper article (2 April 2025):
The government is increasing tax rates on people's incomes by 2% and on business profits by 4%. These increases will be introduced next month. No further tax increases are planned.

Appendix 3 — Extract from PF's statements of financial position ($000):
                    2025    2026 (forecast)
Non-current assets:  500    1000
Current assets:       50      60
Inventories:          10      30
Current liabilities:  40      50
Bank loans:           40     500
Retained profit:      60     100
ms:
Award 1 mark for each advantage/disadvantage (max 2 advantages / 2 disadvantages). Award a maximum of 1 additional mark for each explanation applied to context.

Relevant advantages:
- Limited liability — as the original investment of $100 000 as well as his personal possessions are safe
- More capital / easier to raise finance — as he can sell shares to fund the building of the new factory
- Continuity — if Philip decides to leave the shoe making business, then PF will still exist
- May be able to keep control — because he can decide whether to sell shares to expand the business

Relevant disadvantages:
- He would not be able to keep all the profits/pay dividends — from the manufacture of rubber shoes
- No privacy / will have to share some financial details — from his forecast statement of financial position
- Legal restrictions in setting up the business — which he would not have when he set up the business 10 years ago
- Owner may not now have complete control / making all the decisions / being his own boss — such as where to locate the new factory

Application context: rubber shoes; natural rubber raw material; build a new factory; sells in a mass market; increase in taxes; bank loan for the new factory; sister wants to invest in the business; $100 000; wants to grow the business; produce a new range of shoes; operates in a very competitive market; started 10 years ago; Appendix 3 data.

text:
Consider each of the following three methods PF could use to motivate its employees. Which method should PF use? Justify your answer.
• Paying bonuses
• Piece-rate
• Job rotation

Philip Flop (PF) — Case Study Summary

Philip started PF 10 years ago as a sole trader in country X. PF makes shoes out of natural rubber. Philip used $100 000 of his own money to start up PF. The business has been very successful. "Natural rubber from local forests is used in the production of all our shoes. We use sustainable sources of raw materials unlike our competitors which use imported artificial rubber. Buy your first pair today and you will never buy a different brand again!"

Appendix 3 — Extract from PF's statements of financial position ($000):
                    2025    2026 (forecast)
Non-current assets:  500    1000
Current assets:       50      60

ms:
L3 (9–12): Sound application, detailed discussion of two or more methods, well-justified recommendation with reasons why alternatives rejected.
L2 (5–8): Sound application, detailed discussion of at least one method, judgement with some justification.
L1 (1–4): Limited application, limited discussion, simple judgement with limited justification.

Paying bonuses:
+ Flexible — higher pay if production team increase output of shoes, ensuring they each work harder
+ May bring pay up to the same rate paid by local businesses for similar work — employees less likely to leave, lowering PF's recruitment costs
- May cause disagreements if only some of the 20 employees are working hard — seen as unfair
- Paying a bonus is likely to mean profits are lower — may limit retained profit for expansion
- Can become expected; if not paid, employees become demotivated — reducing productivity

Piece-rate:
+ Wages increase if higher output, so workers motivated to produce more shoes in shorter time — increasing efficiency
- If work is rushed to obtain more wages, quality of shoes might suffer — poor reputation, fewer repeat customers, lower revenue

- May be seen as unfair if different jobs produce more output — motivation may reduce

- Bonus: adds extra to wages for work producing shoes, encourages harder work. Piece-rate may be difficult to calculate as employees do different jobs. Job rotation may be difficult if tasks are very different.
- Piece-rate: employees who work harder producing shoes rewarded with higher wages — based on Taylor's theory of motivation.
- Job rotation: only method that makes job of producing shoes more interesting and less boring. Money motivates only for a short time then effects decrease.

Cap at Level 2 without a justified recommendation.

text: Using Appendix 3 and other information, consider PF's financial position in 2025 and forecast financial position in 2026. Do you think Philip's sister should invest in PF? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
caseStudy:
Philip Flop (PF) — Case Study Summary

Philip started PF 10 years ago as a sole trader in country X. PF makes shoes out of natural rubber. Philip used $100 000 of his own money to start up PF. The business has been very successful. Last year Philip changed PF from a sole trader business to a private limited company because he wanted to grow the business.

PF employs 20 workers to make the shoes. They are paid a weekly wage based on the number of hours worked. Philip often has to recruit new production workers as the jobs are boring. Other local businesses pay a higher wage for similar work. Philip needs to improve the motivation of PF's employees and has to decide the best way to do this.

Philip wants to build a new factory to produce a new range of shoes. PF's products will still be made from natural rubber which is grown in the local area. The bank has agreed to provide a loan to finance the building of the new factory.

Philip needs to choose a suitable location for the new factory and is considering: availability of raw materials, transport links, and government influence.

PF operates in a very competitive market. Philip will need to make a decision about how to promote the new range of shoes in a mass market.

Philip's sister is a successful entrepreneur and is considering investing in PF. She is using the extracts from PF's statements of financial position to help her decide.

Appendix 1 — Advertisement for PF's shoes:
"Natural rubber from local forests is used in the production of all our shoes. We use sustainable sources of raw materials unlike our competitors which use imported artificial rubber. Buy your first pair today and you will never buy a different brand again!"

Appendix 2 — Newspaper article (2 April 2025):
The government is increasing tax rates on people's incomes by 2% and on business profits by 4%. These increases will be introduced next month. No further tax increases are planned.

Appendix 3 — Extract from PF's statements of financial position ($000):
                    2025    2026 (forecast)
Non-current assets:  500    1000
Current assets:       50      60
Inventories:          10      30
Current liabilities:  40      50
Bank loans:           40     500
Retained profit:      60     100
ms:
L3 (9–12): Sound application, detailed discussion of both statements, well-justified recommendation including whether or not Philip's sister should invest.
L2 (5–8): Sound application, detailed discussion of at least one statement, judgement with some justification.
L1 (1–4): Limited application, limited discussion, simple judgement with limited justification.

Basic points:
- Non-current assets are forecast to increase by $500 000
- Inventories are forecast to increase by $20 000
- Long-term bank loans are forecast to increase by $460 000
- Retained profit is forecast to increase by $40 000 to $100 000 in 2026

Key calculations:
- Current ratio 2025: 50/40 = 1.25
- Current ratio 2026 (forecast): 60/50 = 1.2
- Acid test ratio 2025: (50-10)/40 = 40/40 = 1.0
- Acid test ratio 2026 (forecast): (60-30)/50 = 30/50 = 0.6

More developed points:
- Current ratio 2025 of 1.25 could be considered low — better to be nearer 2 — shows business may struggle to pay short-term debts with sufficient liquidity
- Current ratio forecast 2026 is lower than 2025 and is a cause for concern — may mean business has expanded too quickly and may have cash flow problems
- Low acid test ratio for 2026 of 0.6 suggests business is likely to have liquidity problems after new factory is built
- Expansion appears to be mainly funded by large bank loan of $460 000 — interest repayments will result in large increase in expenses — possibly reducing profitability

Recommendation justifications:
- Should invest: non-current assets forecast to nearly double — building of new factory mainly financed by bank loan. Bank would not grant such a big loan without confidence in PF's success. This should reassure Philip's sister that investment will provide good returns.
- Should not invest: forecast statement suggests significant liquidity problems — expected fall in current ratio of 0.05 and expected fall in acid test ratio of 0.4 suggests cash flow problems in the future.

Cap at Level 2 without a justified recommendation.

• Lack of knowledge
caseStudy:
Tennis and Sports Equipment (TSE) — Case Study Summary

TSE is a successful multinational company with its head office in country P. TSE has factories in 10 countries producing high-quality sports equipment. It sells its products in 30 countries and plans to enter a new market in another country. TSE has many stakeholder groups with different objectives.

TSE uses market research in the countries where its products are sold. There are many different sports played in these 30 countries and some sports are popular in only one country.

Raw materials, such as plastic and rubber, are used to make the sports equipment. These are often produced near to TSE's factories. All purchases of raw materials are currently made by the head office in country P. However, TSE's directors are considering whether to allow the factory managers in each country to purchase raw materials locally.

TSE's Human Resources Director knows that having a well-motivated workforce is important as it reduces absenteeism and lowers labour turnover. Most of TSE's production employees are skilled and all work full time. Some of TSE's factories use new technology and have an automated flow production line. The country has enjoyed several years of increasing economic growth. However, country P is now moving into the recession stage of the business cycle.                   Company A    Company B

Cultural differences:
- There may be different preferences for types of sports played in a market in another country — TSE may need to adapt its sports equipment to the ones required for this market — may increase development costs
- Possibly need to adapt packaging/marketing/advertising to cope with differences in culture — may increase marketing costs
- May not be able to compete with existing suppliers of sports equipment that already recognise cultural differences — customers may be brand loyal to locally produced products
- May not produce different products for a new market, so may reduce opportunities for economies of scale — possibly increasing unit costs

- TSE may not be aware of the shopping habits of customers — may need to use different distribution channels — may be difficult to become established with retailers in a new market

caseStudy:
Tennis and Sports Equipment (TSE) — Case Study Summary

TSE is a successful multinational company with its head office in country P. TSE has factories in 10 countries producing high-quality sports equipment. It sells its products in 30 countries and plans to enter a new market in another country. TSE has many stakeholder groups with different objectives.

TSE uses market research in the countries where its products are sold. There are many different sports played in these 30 countries and some sports are popular in only one country.

Raw materials, such as plastic and rubber, are used to make the sports equipment. These are often produced near to TSE's factories. All purchases of raw materials are currently made by the head office in country P. However, TSE's directors are considering whether to allow the factory managers in each country to purchase raw materials locally.

TSE's Human Resources Director knows that having a well-motivated workforce is important as it reduces absenteeism and lowers labour turnover. Most of TSE's production employees are skilled and all work full time. Some of TSE's factories use new technology and have an automated flow production line. However, to remain competitive TSE needs to make sure all of its factories are as efficient as possible.

TSE sells 30% of its total output in country P. The directors want to increase market share in country P and plan to take over a competitor. Appendix 3 includes information about two companies TSE could take over.

Appendix 1 — Advertisement for TSE:
"Need new sports equipment so you can be the best at your sport? Whatever your sport, badminton, football or tennis, we have the most up-to-date equipment. From balls to bats we produce it all at a range of prices. Be the best and choose TSE!"

Appendix 2 — Newspaper article (1 May 2025):
The country has enjoyed several years of increasing economic growth. However, country P is now moving into the recession stage of the business cycle. Businesses will be affected in either positive ways or negative ways. Unemployment is starting to rise and it is expected this will continue for the next year.

Appendix 3 — Extracts from income statements for 2024 for the two companies TSE could take over in country P:
                  Company A    Company B
Revenue:           $100m        $200m
Cost of sales:      $40m         $90m
Expenses:           $40m         $60m
ms:
L3 (9–12): Sound application, detailed discussion of both companies, well-justified recommendation with reasons why alternative company was rejected.
L2 (5–8): Sound application, detailed discussion of one company, judgement with some justification.
L1 (1–4): Limited application, limited discussion, simple judgement with limited justification.

Simple statements:
- Company B has twice as much revenue at $200m
- Company A has less than half the cost of sales compared to Company B, a difference of $50m
- Company B has higher cost of sales at $90m
- The expenses are less than twice as much for Company B at $60m
- Lower revenue means Company A is probably smaller than Company B

Key calculations:
- Gross profit of Company A: $100m - $40m = $60m
- Gross profit margin of Company A: 60/100 x 100 = 60%
- Gross profit of Company B: $200m - $90m = $110m
- Gross profit margin of Company B: 110/200 x 100 = 55%
- Profit of Company A: $60m - $40m = $20m
- Profit margin of Company A: 20/100 x 100 = 20%
- Profit of Company B: $110m - $60m = $50m
- Profit margin of Company B: 50/200 x 100 = 25%

Recommendation justifications:
- TSE should take over Company A: it has a 5% higher gross profit margin than Company B, suggesting it is more efficient in its management of variable costs. It is a smaller competitor with lower revenue at $100m and therefore could require a lower amount of capital to take over. TSE should not take over Company B as it may need to borrow a much higher amount of capital.
- TSE should take over Company B: it has much higher revenue suggesting it is a larger competitor and will better help TSE achieve the aim of increasing its market share. It also has a 5% higher profit margin than Company A.

Cap at Level 2 without a justified recommendation.

text: Explain two drawbacks for EP of having a tall organisational structure.
context: EP has a tall organisational structure with 6 levels and 84 employees including 50 production employees and 10 production supervisors. EP is a private limited company making high-quality pottery products in country Y.
caseStudy: EP is a private limited company set up 40 years ago in country Y. It manufactures pottery products including plates, cups and bowls. EP has a reputation for producing high-quality products. The Managing Director is considering the best way to increase the added value of EP products by either increasing prices or reducing raw material costs. Raw materials are purchased locally as imported raw materials are of lower quality. EP operates in a very competitive market with many substitutes including plastic or bamboo. Consumer spending patterns changing in country Y affecting EP sales. EP advertises in newspapers and magazines only. EP does not have a website and only sells to retail shops in country Y. EP needs a new Marketing Manager — the Managing Director thinks EP should recruit externally. New Marketing Manager will consider: Advertising using social media; Emailing special offers to existing customers; Setting up a website. Managing Director wants to increase factory efficiency by either improving labour skills or introducing more automation. Both methods need additional finance. Appendix 2 org chart: 6 levels, 84 total employees — 50 production employees, 10 production supervisors. Appendix 3: Product A (Price $10, Sales 20000 units, Total cost $140000, Profit $60000, GPM 50%, PM 30%, Demand +10%). Product B (Price $40, Sales 10000 units, Total cost $350000, Profit $50000, GPM 62.5%, PM 12.5%, Demand +20%).
ms: Award 1 mark per drawback (max 2). Award max 3 additional marks per explanation including one applied to context. Drawbacks: Communication slower — long chain of command — longer for messages to reach production employees — more chance of errors about pottery production; Misunderstandings occur — more people messages passed through; Senior managers more remote — less aware of views of 50 production employees — more likely to feel demotivated; Decision making slower — more levels — react to customer changes more slowly; Narrow span of control — fewer delegation opportunities; Increasing managerial costs — more managers needed as 6 levels. Application: pottery, cups, plates, bowls, 40 years, new Marketing Manager, Managing Director, 84 employees, 6 levels, external recruitment, high-quality products, private limited company, Appendix 2.

text: Explain four differences between a partnership and a limited company.
context: Benjy plans to start BB as a business partnership with his father and sister, each investing $30,000. Benjy is deciding on the best legal structure as the business may need more investment as it expands. No application marks for this question.
caseStudy:
Benjy's Builders (BB) — Case Study Summary

Benjy is experienced in building houses. He worked for a building company for 15 years in country X. Benjy has decided to start his own house-building business called BB. His main objective is to make a profit. He plans to invite his father and sister to invest in the business partnership — all three will each invest $30,000 to start BB. Benjy thinks BB may need more investment as it expands. Benjy will be the manager, as his father and sister do not want to be involved in running BB.

Benjy's son has a physical disability. As there were not many houses suitable for his son's needs, Benjy decided to build a specially designed house. This gave him the idea to specialise in building houses designed to meet the needs of people with disabilities. He does not know the demand for this type of house and plans to carry out market research to estimate the size of the market. There are currently no other businesses in country X which specialise in building houses for people with disabilities.

The houses will be designed for the individual needs of each customer — BB will use job production. The houses will be built of timber and have metal roofs. The timber BB uses will be imported. Good-quality materials will always be used so the houses are of the highest quality. Benjy needs to decide which pricing method to use when selling the houses.

Benjy plans to employ 8 workers with specialist building skills and 2 unskilled workers, who will need to be told what to do. He will need to decide which leadership style to use with his employees.

Benjy also has to decide which type of house to build first, to be used in advertising and available for potential customers to visit. House A is designed for people with visual difficulties and House B is designed for people with physical difficulties.

Appendix 1 — Search results for the number of people with disabilities in country X:
- The population in country X is 50 million.
- 1 in 4 of the population has a disability.
- 10% have visual difficulties.
- 30% have physical difficulties and may have restrictions in their movement or are wheelchair users.

Appendix 2 — Financial information for the two options for BB's first house ($000s):
House A (visual difficulties): Timber costs $10,000; Labour costs $15,000; All other costs $38,000; Forecast selling price $70,000.
House B (physical difficulties): Timber costs $20,000; Labour costs $20,000; All other costs $60,000; Forecast selling price $110,000.

Appendix 3 — Newspaper article from Main News, September 2023:
The exchange rate for the currency of country X has depreciated. This has resulted in a change in the price of imported food and manufactured goods, such as wheelchairs. The depreciation will also have a big effect on spending, especially for people with disabilities who purchase imported specialist equipment to help them. The price of imported building materials, such as timber, may also change due to the depreciation in the exchange rate.
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per difference (max 4) + max 1 additional mark per explanation of the difference. NO application marks for this question.

Differences (any four):
- Liability — partnership has unlimited liability (personal possessions can be taken to pay business debts) / company has limited liability (personal possessions not at risk)
- Sources of capital — partnership has capital from owners' savings / company can sell shares
- Legal formalities — partnership has no legal documents to complete to start / company has to register and complete legal documents
- Legal identity — partnership is unincorporated with no separate legal identity between owner and business / company is incorporated with separate legal identity
- Continuity — partnership ends with death of a partner / company shares can be transferred so continues even after death of shareholders
- Visibility of financial statements — partnership statements are kept private / company statements published (PLC) or can be accessed (Ltd)
- Management — partnership often managed by the partners / company directors make decisions and may or may not be shareholders

Example: 'Liability is different (1). In a partnership the owners have unlimited liability which means personal possessions can be taken to pay business debts, whereas a company has limited liability and personal possessions are safe (1).'

text:
Consider three leadership styles that Benjy could use when managing BB. Which leadership style should Benjy use? Justify your answer.
• Autocratic
• Democratic
• Laissez-faire
context: Benjy will manage BB, employing 8 workers with specialist building skills and 2 unskilled workers who will need to be told what to do. Benjy needs to decide which leadership style to use with his employees.

Benjy's Builders (BB) — Case Study Summary

Benjy is experienced in building houses. He worked for a building company for 15 years in country X. Benjy has decided to start his own house-building business called BB. Appendix 3 — Newspaper article from Main News, September 2023:
The exchange rate for the currency of country X has depreciated. This has resulted in a change in the price of imported food and manufactured goods, such as wheelchairs. The depreciation will also have a big effect on spending, especially for people with disabilities who purchase imported specialist equipment to help them. The price of imported building materials, such as timber, may also change due to the depreciation in the exchange rate.
ms:
12 marks. Levels-based marking.

Level 3 (9-12): Sound application, detailed discussion of TWO OR MORE leadership styles, well-justified recommendation including why alternative styles were rejected. Top marks if all three discussed in detail in context.
Level 2 (5-8): Sound application, detailed discussion of at least one style, judgement with some justification. Top marks if two or more discussed in detail and applied to the case.
Level 1 (1-4): Limited application, limited discussion, simple judgement. Top marks if all three outlined in context.

Autocratic: Manager expects to be in charge, all employees follow orders — e.g. which timber should be used; Benjy keeps himself separate from the 10 employees; Communication one-way, no opportunity to comment — can be demotivating; Benjy makes all decisions, keeps information to himself — 2 unskilled employees need to be told what to do; Decision-making quicker than democratic.

Democratic: 8 skilled employees motivated — gets employees involved in decision making; Future plans may be shared and discussed before final decision — employees more accepting of change; Communication both downward and upward — allows experience of 8 skilled employees to be considered, possibly better decisions; Employees feel more involved — less likely to leave — reducing recruitment costs; May be time-consuming to ask employees — reduces work carried out; Unpopular decisions may still need to be made, ideas ignored.

Laissez-faire: Main objectives shared then employees organise own work and take decisions without interference — can be motivating, employees feel valued and trusted; Communication between manager and employees can be difficult — manager has little involvement; Employees can be creative with fresh ideas about building houses more quickly; Not suitable if clear direction and consistent approach to a certain specification is needed.

Valid recommendations:
- Autocratic: gives clear instructions followed by 10 employees — may not work well together / mistakes may be made if left to make own decisions (laissez-faire); they won't have all the business information needed to make valid suggestions (democratic).
- Democratic: close working relationship with 10 employees, easy to listen to opinions before deciding — motivates employees as they feel valued.
- Laissez-faire: each customer has very different needs — more creativity and problem solving achieved if employees make own decisions building specialist houses for people with disabilities — gains more customers.

Cap at Level 2 without a justified recommendation.

Cost-plus — Advantages: easy to apply, different mark-up for different houses depending on demand; each house makes a profit as different costs covered by price charged. Penetration — Advantages: lower price than competitors attracts customers, increases sales; helps ensure successful launch into new market for people with disabilities; market share should build up quickly. Disadvantages: low price could mean low profit per house; customers who bought early may expect prices to remain low and not purchase when price rises later.

Skimming — Advantages: customer may think the adapted house is high quality; high R&D costs for adaptations quickly recovered; house is unique so customers may expect to pay high prices — high profits before competitors enter. Disadvantages: high price may put off potential customers; high price/profits may encourage competitors to quickly enter the market, taking away BB's advantage of being first.

- Cost-plus: each house is different, uses different amounts of materials for individual needs — ensures a profit is made for each house. Penetration not needed as no competitors exist in country X. Skimming not appropriate as Benjy will not want to maximise profit from people with disabilities given his own son has a disability.
- Penetration: new house design — get the house builder established in the market and well-known, building good reputation and increasing future sales.
- Skimming: specially designed house is a new idea and BB will be first in the market — high prices should be charged to gain maximum profit before competitors enter.

text: Explain two advantages and two disadvantages of PH being a public limited company.
context: PH is a large public limited company based in country Z, operating successfully for 50 years, producing protective hats with a reputation for high quality. PH plans to expand by opening factories in other countries and become a multinational company.
caseStudy:
Protective Hats (PH) — Case Study Summary

PH is a large public limited company based in country Z. It has been operating successfully for 50 years. PH produces a range of protective hats for employees working on construction sites, in factories or mines. It has a reputation for producing high-quality products and sells its hats around the world.

PH is currently the market leader in country Z. To remain competitive PH regularly carries out market research to find out if new products are needed. PH needs to ensure its market research data is accurate, so that it can develop the best new protective hats.

PH's only factory is in country Z. It has 100 production employees. They work on a flow production line and carry out the same tasks every day. PH pays these employees the minimum wage and there have been complaints about working conditions. Some of the employees are considering becoming members of a trade union.

PH's directors plan to expand the company by opening factories in other countries to produce protective hats. They think there are many benefits for PH of becoming a multinational company. They are aware that there is growing demand for protective hats in many developing countries where construction and manufacturing industries are expected to continue to have strong growth in the next 10 years.

Appendix 1 — Advertisement for PH's products:
"PH's protective hats will protect your employees when at work. We supply many of the leading construction, manufacturing and mining companies across the world. High quality is guaranteed. PH's hats can be ordered online from our website."

Appendix 2 — Email to PH's Managing Director from PH's Human Resources Director (1 October 2023):
"After reviewing our current training, I think we need to increase the training we provide to new employees. Existing employees would also benefit from additional training as there have been issues with motivation. I know there are plans to introduce new equipment into the flow production line. When is this likely to happen? Can we please meet to discuss these issues?"

Appendix 3 — PH's financial data for 2021 and 2022:
                    2021      2022
Revenue:            $100m     $125m
Profit:              $20m      $20m
Gross profit margin: 60%       65%
Profit margin:       20%       16%
ms:
8 marks. Award 1 mark per advantage/disadvantage (max 2 advantages, max 2 disadvantages) + max 1 additional mark per explanation applied to context.

Advantages (any two):
- Can sell shares to the public — attractive to prospective shareholders given PH's long history of high-quality products
- Limited liability — protects shareholders' assets when expanding into other countries
- Continuity — shares passed on if shareholders die, allowing the company to exist for over 50 years
- Higher status may make it easier to borrow from banks
- Rapid expansion possible/can raise large amounts of capital
- Incorporated/separate legal identity

Disadvantages (any two):
- Legal formalities — for this business manufacturing protective hats
- Accounts must be published — may be viewed by competitors wanting to become market leader
- Divorce between ownership and control/potential conflict between managers and shareholders
- Risk of takeover/no control over who buys shares
- Directors' decisions may be influenced by major investors seeking their own objectives

Application: protective hats; construction sites; construction/mining workers; plan to expand by opening factories in other countries; remain market leader; long history of high-quality products; 50 years in business; becoming a multinational company.

Example: 'A public limited company can sell shares to the public (1), and this makes it easier to raise capital for investment in new factories to produce its protective hats (app).'

Level 3 (9-12): Sound application, detailed discussion of BOTH ways, well-justified recommendation including why the alternative way was rejected.

Quality control — Advantages: products checked at end of production line, eliminates faults before customer receives protective hats; less training required for the 100 workers as inspectors check quality before hats leave factory. Disadvantages: raises costs as inspectors need to be employed; identifies faulty hats at the end but doesn't identify where the fault occurred; if fault not identified, faulty process not eliminated — higher costs if hats need to be scrapped/reworked; employees may be demotivated as checks aren't their responsibility — may cause more careless errors.

Quality assurance — Advantages: products checked at every stage, eliminates faults before passing to next stage — reduces faults at end; fewer customer complaints; reduced wastage costs from fewer scrapped hats; can make workers feel trusted, improving motivation. Disadvantages: expensive to train employees to check own work; relies on employee reliability and commitment; takes longer to produce hats as each worker checks their own work; components/raw materials need approved standard — may restrict suppliers, increasing costs; employees may expect higher pay for the checks given they're currently on minimum wage.

Valid recommendations:
- Quality control: if the process is simple, inspectors can carry out a simple end check. The 100 production workers don't need training to check their own work (saving training costs), and production is faster than quality assurance where workers check at every stage.
- Quality assurance: each stage checked so less likely a faulty product reaches customers than quality control. Keeps good brand image/reputation, very important for protective hats. Ensures faults don't need repairing, reducing scrapped product costs.

Focus group (existing customers) — Advantages: questions people already familiar with the products (construction/mining workers) — more likely to gain detailed/honest info about existing products to help develop a new hat; interaction between members helps researchers understand reasons for opinions. Online survey (5 questions) — Advantages: results automatically analysed/presented via IT — quicker/cheaper to collate; fast with quicker response than postal survey — can be emailed to existing customers using existing email addresses; cheaper than interviews/postal questionnaires — no personnel/postage costs; larger sample from different parts of the world. - Focus group most accurate: uses existing customers already familiar with the hats, allowing detailed information gathering. Online surveys may not sample widely enough and are restricted to 5 questions; government statistics may be out of date for a fast-moving mining industry.

Produce in low-cost countries: Low rents reduce total costs — may lead to lower prices, increasing sales via competitiveness; Low production costs may allow higher profit margins than 2022's 16% if prices stay the same; Producing hats in countries with low labour costs — lower unit costs, more competitive/increased sales in other markets.
